title: Improved Quantum Codes with Transversal T Gates
abstract: In this work, we study quantum CSS codes with transversal $T$ gates. Here, $T$ gate transversality is meant in the strongest sense; the application of physical $T$ to every physical qubit yields logical $T$ on every logical qubit, without Clifford corrections. Despite the importance of the $T$ gate in fault-tolerant quantum computation, the parameters of asymptotic families of such codes have not been improved since the work of Hastings and Haah in 2017, and Haah in 2018. In this work, we significantly broaden the achievable parameters of quantum code families with transversal $T$ gates, both expanding the regime of achievable polynomial rate and distance, and constructing such codes with constant rate and growing distance; this is the first time the latter has been achieved, even when allowing Clifford corrections after the transversal $T$ gate. These are also the first codes achieving $γ\to 0$ for a code with a transversal $T$ gate, where $γ$ is the overhead exponent of magic state distillation.   To do this, we develop a framework of divisible decreasing monomial codes, punctured at a downward-closed set on the Boolean hypercube to create logical qubits. We prove a closed-form expression for the distance of such a code punctured at such a set, which may be of independent interest. We first instantiate this with an explicit construction based on weighted Reed-Muller codes, puncturing at low Hamming-weight points, and then with a randomised construction, where a small random set of points is protected from the puncturing to save quantum code distance, achieving improved parameters.
summary: This paper advances the theory of quantum error-correcting codes by improving the achievable parameters for codes supporting transversal T gates. Using advanced algebraic constructions based on punctured monomial codes, the authors achieve constant rate and growing distance for the first time in this context. This work significantly pushes the theoretical boundaries for building scalable, fault-tolerant quantum computers.
main_problem: The primary goal is to improve the achievable parameters (rate and distance) of quantum error-correcting codes that support transversal T gates, which is crucial for fault-tolerant quantum computation.
main_result: The authors significantly broaden the achievable parameters by constructing codes that achieve constant rate and growing distance for the first time in this setting, and achieving $\gamma 	o 0$ for the overhead exponent.
method: The work develops a theoretical framework using divisible decreasing monomial codes punctured at specific sets on the Boolean hypercube, and applies this to weighted Reed-Muller codes and randomized constructions.
model_or_system: The study focuses on quantum CSS codes, specifically analyzing the constraints imposed by requiring a transversal T gate application across all physical qubits to yield the logical T gate.
key_observables: Achievable code parameters, including rate ($\alpha$), distance exponent ($ eta$), and the overhead exponent ($\gamma$) for magic state distillation.
important_parameters: The regime of polynomial rate/distance, and the constant rate/growing distance regime, particularly for $R \in (0, 1/3)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis is primarily restricted to stabilizer codes, although the authors suggest potential extensions beyond this class.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the boundaries of achievable dimension and distance exponents $(\alpha,  eta)$ for explicit versus non-explicit constructions. Figure 2 plots the boundary in the constant-rate regime.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the theoretical framework using punctured decreasing monomial codes, derives a closed-form distance expression, and then instantiates this with explicit constructions (like weighted Reed-Muller codes) and randomized methods to prove improved asymptotic bounds.
why_interesting: While focused on abstract coding theory, the results provide concrete, improved bounds on the resource overheads (like distillation exponents) required for fault-tolerant quantum computation, which is a major theoretical bottleneck in quantum information science.
